CHENNAI: AIADMK general secretary Edappadi K Palaniswami on Friday warned of  protests  if the Tamil Nadu government is not withdrawing cases registered against seven  farmers  in  Tiruvannamalai  district who have also been detained under the  Goondas Act . 
"The government should stop indulging in politics of violence and withdraw the cases and fulfil the demands," he said in a statement.
The farmers had been holding non-violent protests against a government order to acquire 3,300 acres of agricultural land in nine village panchayats of Cheyyar assembly constituency in Tiruvannamalai district for expansion of SIPCOT industrial estate. The district unit of the AIADMK held protests on October 4.
Palaniswami alleged that the government had registered a series of cases against youths and farmers to reduce the intensity of the struggle. "Citing series of cases against the farmers who have no previous cases, the government has slapped the Goondas Act against seven of them on the grounds that they disturb peace. The areas look like a battlefield," the former CM said.
He accused the government of placing barbed wire as on the borders and positioning riot control vehicles like Vajra to curtail the protests. 
The former chief minister said his government had given up the acquisition plan upon finding that multi-cropping was practised there.
The AIADMK leader said that his government had permitted the agitations instigated by the DMK, even extended security cover to the protesters and realised their just demands. 
"The DMK government uses the police force to take revenge on the political opponents and suppress the protests of government staff and farmers," he said.

"The government should stop indulging in politics of violence, withdraw the cases, and fulfill the demands," he stated.

The AIADMK's district unit held protests regarding this issue on October 4.

He also claimed that the government, citing these new cases, had invoked the Goondas Act against seven farmers with no prior offenses, asserting they were disturbing peace. The former Chief Minister added that the areas affected now "look like a battlefield."

He further accused the government of deploying barbed wire and riot control vehicles like Vajra to suppress the protests. Palaniswami noted that his previous government had abandoned a similar land acquisition plan after discovering that multi-cropping was practiced in the area.

text1: Spotlight, the current affairs strand made by BBC Northern Ireland, has been garlanded with awards during its 43-year history. But I think it has lost the run of itself after seeing its programme a week ago about the 2006 killing of a Sinn Féin official, Denis Donaldson. His death followed soon after he had admitted to being a British agent for the best part of 20 years. Its central claim was that Gerry Adams, the party's leader, had been responsible for ordering the murder. And such is the status of Spotlight that the allegation made headlines in Ireland's leading newspapers, plus one or two UK nationals. The programme, Spy in the IRA, relied on the "evidence" of an anonymous single source. His identity and voice were concealed "because of fears for his safety." He was said to be a former IRA volunteer and Sinn Féin member who had himself become an informer for the British secret services. His "exclusive interview" was hyped up by Spotlight's reporter, Jennifer O'Leary, in a pre-broadcast preview article in which she wrote: "For months, I've been in contact with a man, referred to in the programme as ‘Martin'". On screen, however, his statements lacked any semblance of truthfulness. They amounted to staccato answers to leading questions. There was not a scintilla of supporting evidence for his claims about Adams, who is a member of the Irish parliament, having sanctioned the murder. As a journalistic exercise, the programme looked to be wholly inadequate. And it didn't take long for its allegation about Adams's involvement to unravel. That wasn't too unsurprising since the Real IRA - one of the so-called dissident groups antagonistic to Sinn Féin - had admitted its responsibity for killing Donaldson some three years after his death. First, Adams issued a statement, reported on the BBC website, saying: "I specifically and categorically refute these unsubstantiated allegations", which he saw as an attempt to smear him. Second, Adams's solicitor followed up with another unequivocal rebuttal, as reported by the Guardian, about his client having "no knowledge of and... no involvement whatsoever in the killing of Denis Donaldson." Third, the Guardian reported on Friday that Donaldson's relatives had rejected the Spotlight claim. A solicitor acting for them and speaking on their behalf called it "absolute nonsense." Fourth, the clincher: the Sunday Times's Irish edition ran a story about the Irish police (the gardai) seeking the extradition from Scotland of two men in connection with Donaldson's murder who are not connected to either the now-disbanded Provisional IRA nor Sinn Féin. The article further stated: "Gardai say they have no evidence to support claims that the killing was sanctioned by Adams." It quoted a garda source as saying: "We have no evidence to put to Gerry Adams. The investigation team would have no reason to invite him in for questioning or even attempt to arrest him... we have built up a detailed picture of those involved in Donaldson's murder. Adams does not feature." So where does that leave Spotlight's exclusive? I sent these questions to the BBC Northern Ireland press office earlier today: Given that the "evidence" of the source known as "Martin" has been rubbished by Adams, his solicitor, Donaldson's family, and the gardai, does the BBC still stand by the claims he made? On reflection, do the people responsible for the programme really think Martin's allegations were credible? What steps were taken to ensure that he wasn't a fantasist? Is the BBC happy with relying on a single source making controversial allegations, which appears to contravene the corporation's guidelines? Was the documentary run past the BBC's editorial and standards department prior to transmission? Finally, given that a Spotlight in 2014 levelled contested claims at Adams, does it not worry the BBC that it could be accused of attempting to smear the Sinn Fein leader? In response, a BBC spokesperson issued a statement saying: "The programme dealt with matters of great public interest and fully met the BBC's editorial standards. The BBC stands by its journalism." NB: I have previously written for Sinn Féin's newspaper, An Phoblacht.

Has BBC's Spotlight Gone Too Far? Questions Arise Over Adams Murder Allegation

Spotlight, BBC Northern Ireland's acclaimed current affairs program with a 43-year history of awards, seems to have strayed, in my opinion, after its recent broadcast concerning the 2006 killing of Sinn Féin official Denis Donaldson. Donaldson's death occurred shortly after he admitted to being a British agent for nearly two decades. The program's central assertion was that Sinn Féin leader Gerry Adams had ordered the murder. Given Spotlight's standing, this allegation made headlines in Ireland's leading newspapers and even some in the UK.

The program, titled "Spy in the IRA," relied on the "evidence" of a single, anonymous source. His identity and voice were disguised "because of fears for his safety." He was presented as a former IRA volunteer and Sinn Féin member who himself had become an informer for the British secret services. Spotlight reporter Jennifer O'Leary hyped his "exclusive interview" in a pre-broadcast preview article, stating, "For months, I've been in contact with a man, referred to in the programme as 'Martin'." However, his on-screen statements lacked any semblance of truthfulness, amounting to staccato answers to leading questions. There wasn't a shred of supporting evidence for his claims that Adams, a member of the Irish parliament, had sanctioned the murder.

As a journalistic endeavor, the program appeared entirely inadequate. It didn't take long for the allegation about Adams's involvement to fall apart. This wasn't particularly surprising, as the Real IRA—one of the dissident groups opposed to Sinn Féin—had claimed responsibility for Donaldson's killing about three years after his death.

First, Adams issued a statement, reported on the BBC website, unequivocally refuting "these unsubstantiated allegations," which he viewed as an attempt to smear him. Second, Adams's solicitor followed up with another clear rebuttal, reported by The Guardian, stating his client had "no knowledge of and... no involvement whatsoever in the killing of Denis Donaldson." Third, The Guardian reported on Friday that Donaldson's relatives had rejected the Spotlight claim, with their solicitor calling it "absolute nonsense." Fourth, and most conclusively, the Irish edition of The Sunday Times ran a story about the Irish police (the Gardaí) seeking the extradition from Scotland of two men in connection with Donaldson's murder. These individuals are not connected to the now-disbanded Provisional IRA or Sinn Féin. The article further stated: "Gardai say they have no evidence to support claims that the killing was sanctioned by Adams." It quoted a Garda source as saying, "We have no evidence to put to Gerry Adams. The investigation team would have no reason to invite him in for questioning or even attempt to arrest him... we have built up a detailed picture of those involved in Donaldson's murder. Adams does not feature."

So, where does that leave Spotlight's exclusive? Earlier today, I sent these questions to the BBC Northern Ireland press office:

Given that the "evidence" from the source known as "Martin" has been discredited by Adams, his solicitor, Donaldson's family, and the Gardaí, does the BBC still stand by his claims?

Upon reflection, do those responsible for the program truly believe Martin's allegations were credible?

What steps were taken to ensure he wasn't a fantasist?

Is the BBC comfortable relying on a single source making controversial allegations, which seems to contravene the corporation's guidelines?

Was the documentary reviewed by the BBC's editorial and standards department before transmission?

Finally, considering that a 2014 Spotlight program also leveled contested claims against Adams, does the BBC not worry about being accused of attempting to smear the Sinn Féin leader?

In response, a BBC spokesperson issued a statement saying: "The programme dealt with matters of great public interest and fully met the BBC's editorial standards. The BBC stands by its journalism."

NB: I have previously contributed to Sinn Féin's newspaper, An Phoblacht.

text1: This month, the Oxford English Dictionary added "bookaholic", "bestie" and "hero's welcome" to its ever-growing collection of words and definitions. Two terms I wish it would revisit? "Undue" and "burden". And then I wish it would send a dictionary to every court in the United States. On Thursday afternoon, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals issued its ruling on a restrictive Texas abortion law. Famously filibustered by Wendy Davis over a marathon 11 hours, HB 2 was eventually signed into law and requires abortion providers to have admitting privileges at hospitals within 30 miles – which isn't a requirement for other health care providers – and unnecessarily restricts the use of non-surgical medical abortions ("the abortion pill"). While those restrictions may sound reasonable enough, they were crafted by Texas Republicans specifically to make abortions harder to get, not to make the procedure safer – abortion is one of the safest procedures around, and both the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the American Medical Association deem the restrictions unnecessary. Adding to the difficulty are the many hospitals in Texas the have denied admitting privileges to abortion providers, making it impossible for the providers to meet the new legal standards. Planned Parenthood and other clinicians challenged the strict new law, of course. So the Fifth Circuit court was tasked with determining if the restrictions, which have effectively shut down at least 20 clinics across Texas including the only two in the vast Rio Grande Valley, placed an "undue burden" on women's health. The court said no. In 2011, 44 clinics performed abortions in Texas. Today, there are 19 – and fewer by the day. When additional regulations go into effect in September, there will be six, maybe seven. That handful of clinics will serve a state of 13 million women with the largest rural population in the United States, in a country where one in three women has an abortion in her lifetime. But back to the dictionary. Under US law, states may pass and enforce abortion regulations so long as they don't place an "undue burden" on women seeking the procedure. The definition of "undue burden", however, is rapidly expanding, as courts seem to take the position that almost nothing is "undue" when it comes to burdening women who need to end their pregnancies. For women in the Rio Grande Valley, the burden is heavy. One of the poorest regions in the United States, Valley residents are overwhelmingly Latino and badly underserved. The Valley shares 1,200 miles of border with Mexico, and has the highest proportion of colonias (unincorporated counties) in the US, with many areas lacking clean water, drainage, functional sewage systems and paved roads. Texas has the highest uninsured population in the nation, with a full 27% – 6.1. million people – lacking coverage. The Valley is even worse off than the rest of the state. As those last two abortion providers in the Valley shut down, the closest clinic is now in San Antonio, some 240 miles away. Getting there requires a car and a four-hour drive across deep Texas roads – if your immigration status even permits you to travel that far, which is not the case for many Valley women. A full day's drive to the clinic also means taking a day off of work, which is a significant difficulty for a low-wage worker in the Valley, which has one of the largest agricultural workforces in the United States. It also necessitates arranging childcare – the majority of women who terminate pregnancies already have at least one child – and scrapping together enough money not only for the procedure itself, but also for transportation there and back and for wages lost. Under Texas law, a woman also has to listen to a script designed to discourage her from terminating at least 24 hours before the procedure. Many women in the Valley are now reportedly going to Mexico to terminate there. According to the Fifth Circuit, that's not unduly burdensome, because even though the new restrictions decrease the number of abortion providers and require women to travel further for procedures, "the burden does not fall on the vast majority of Texas women seeking abortions". When we're talking about women who seek abortions in the Rio Grande Valley, we are largely talking about poor, rural Latina mothers who work long days farming. They are not the vast majority of Texas women. But they are the women who will shoulder this new and increasingly severe burden placed by legislators and judges upon innocent people. The case will likely go to the Supreme Court, which earlier this week heard arguments on whether requiring for-profit companies to include contraception in their health insurance plan placed a "substantial burden" on the company by violating their alleged religious beliefs. That didn't go so well, apparently. There's a decent chance the Court will say, as the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals did, that companies can have religious beliefs, and that it is substantially burdensome to require them to provide women with insurance that covers basic health care. "Burden": it's illuminating to see just how malleable the definition of that word has become – and whose backs we think should bear its weight.

text1: Tony Blair has written to the newly elected president of Kyrgyzstan urging him not to extradite 15 Uzbeks who fled their country after troops opened fire on demonstrators in the southern town of Andijan. They are now wanted as "terrorists" by the authoritarian regime of Uzbekistan. Their plight has become a litmus test for the Kyrgyz president, Kurmanbek Bakiyev, who finds himself at the centre of a strategic tug of war between US, Britain and the EU, eager to encourage western values in central Asia, and Russia, intent on retaining its influence in the former Soviet stronghold. Hundreds of Uzbeks fled across the border with Kyrgyzstan after Uzbek troops opened fire on demonstrators on May 13; 439 of them have since been designated refugees by the UN and found residence in a third country. A further 15 remain at a Kyrgyz detention facility. Uzbekistan seeks their extradition on charges of terrorism, which carry the death penalty. A spokesman for President Bakiyev said yesterday that the 15 detainees had been arrested and their "future would be determined" after an investigation into their conduct ended.
